prompt.context: You are meeting with the head of new product development for Coca Cola to discuss a new delivery platform Coca Cola has developed. Coca Cola does not generally make its delivery platforms – it is usually delivered through fountains or vending machines. But Coca Cola has recently been looking into developing a new vending machine. It's at the first level of screening. It was born out of an idea the engineers at Coca Cola came up with and this executive needs to know whether to use the vending machine or kill the idea. This vending machine can change prices as the temperature changes. If it's hotter outside, the price to the consumer will be higher. If it's cooler, the price goes down accordingly. Assume there is no extra cost to making these vending machines and that they are easily implemented.
prompt.question: How would you evaluate this idea and what is your recommendation?

clarifying_info.a: Yes – about 60% is bought in summer.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current price and cost structure for a can of Coke?
clarifying_info.a: A Coke sells for around $1.00. Costs to produce are: 20 cents manufacturing and 75 cents in marketing, leaving 5 cents profit on each can.

clarifying_info.q: Does Coca Cola expect to make more money from this new vending machine?
clarifying_info.a: No. Coca Cola does not expect to make more money on sales through this vending machine. It expects the high prices in hotter weather and low prices in colder weather to even out to be similar to current revenues.

framework: Supply chain management and demand forecasting: assess whether dynamic pricing stabilizes demand and reduces distribution complexity
Cost structure analysis: evaluate where costs sit (manufacturing vs. marketing) and whether supply chain savings are meaningful
Customer perception and brand risk: consider how Coca Cola's brand positioning interacts with weather-based price changes
Revenue and profitability impact: verify whether the machine changes the overall revenue/profit picture

questions.prompt: What problem might the engineers have been trying to solve when they developed this machine?
questions.guidance: The machine addresses supply chain and demand forecasting problems. Coca Cola sales are highly seasonal (60% in summer), making it difficult to plan manufacturing and distribution. Dynamic pricing could smooth demand curves throughout the year – lower prices in cold weather incentivize purchases off-peak, while higher prices in hot weather capture willingness to pay and reduce the spike. Candidates may also consider freshness/flatness issues (warm-weather Coke going flat faster) or distribution bottlenecks in peak summer season.

questions.prompt: Given that Coca Cola does not expect to make more money, what might they be trying to achieve? Think about the profit tree.
questions.guidance: Even with flat revenues, the benefit lies on the cost side. By stabilizing demand across seasons, Coca Cola can better forecast and smooth out its supply chain, potentially reducing manufacturing and distribution costs. However, candidates should note that manufacturing is only 20 cents out of 95 cents total cost – the dominant cost is marketing (75 cents). Therefore, supply chain savings from smoother demand would be marginal. If Coke wants to cut costs meaningfully, it should look at marketing, not manufacturing or distribution.

math.setup: Cost breakdown per can sold at $1.00: Manufacturing = $0.20, Marketing = $0.75, Profit = $0.05. Manufacturing as % of total cost = 0.20 / 0.95.
steps: Even a significant reduction in manufacturing/distribution costs would have limited impact on total cost given marketing dominates
math.answer: Manufacturing is ~21% of costs; marketing is ~79%. Supply chain savings from this machine would be modest at best.

questions.prompt: What might Coca Cola want to think about before introducing this delivery system? How might people react to it?
questions.guidance: Public perception and brand risk is the critical downside. Coca Cola is an iconic, all-American brand associated with consistency and accessibility. A machine that charges more when it's hot – precisely when people most want a cold drink and are most vulnerable to needing one – could be seen as exploitative price gouging. Consumers may feel cheated. This backlash could damage the brand far more than any supply chain benefit is worth. Candidates should also note that the machine only monitors temperature and adjusts price; it does not itself generate or suppress demand – consumer behavior still drives actual purchase decisions.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Coca Cola weigh before deciding whether to launch this dynamic-pricing vending machine?

Better inventory forecasting lowers waste
Eases distribution planning during peak summer months
Reduces risk of product going flat due to high summer volume

categories.name: Cost Structure

Marketing dominates costs at 75 cents – true cost reduction requires marketing focus

categories.name: Strategic Fit

Is this the right lever vs. addressing marketing cost bloat?
First-mover risk in consumer backlash vs. potential supply chain innovation benefit

recommendation: Do not launch the dynamic-pricing vending machine in its current form
The supply chain benefits are real but modest: smoother demand helps forecasting and distribution, but manufacturing is only ~21% of costs so savings are limited

The brand risk is severe: charging consumers more when it is hottest is misaligned with Coca Cola's all-American, accessible brand identity and will likely trigger a consumer backlash that outweighs any operational gain
risks: Significant public relations and brand damage if the pricing mechanism is perceived as exploitative
Limited financial upside – even perfect demand smoothing saves little given marketing's dominance of the cost structure
The machine does not itself generate demand – it only adjusts price; actual volume still depends on consumer behavior
next_steps: If Coca Cola still wants to improve supply chain economics, explore demand forecasting and distribution optimization without price manipulation
Examine the marketing cost structure (75 cents per can) for savings opportunities, which offers far greater leverage than manufacturing
If dynamic pricing is still attractive, consider piloting in limited markets with careful consumer research and messaging before any broad rollout
